mythologySignificance:
Linked to the peacock (mayil) lore of Mylapore and Parvati’s penance. The temple tank and Panguni festival are city landmarks.

Classical pilgrimage teaching places Kapaleeshwarar Temple, Mylapore within India’s tirtha network: a location where devotion to Lord Shiva (Kapaleeshwarar) & Goddess Karpagambal is believed to ripen vows more readily than in ordinary space. Epic, Puranic, and regional mahatmya literature — not a single uniform text — sustain this sense of sacred geography.
localBeliefs:
In popular pilgrimage memory, Kapaleeshwarar Temple, Mylapore is especially associated with Chennai’s classic Dravidian neighbourhood temple. Guides and elders retell this identity to first-time visitors as the living ‘reason’ the tirtha draws crowds.

Local sthala-purana and priestly teaching at Kapaleeshwarar Temple, Mylapore elaborate how Lord Shiva (Kapaleeshwarar) & Goddess Karpagambal blesses devotees who arrive with vows, gratitude, or grief. Festival days intensify these beliefs through processions, special alankara, and community feeding where practised.

Pilgrims commonly link practical customs — dress, queue, prasadam, and parikrama — with spiritual fruit. Such customs are living belief: they vary by region and should be followed as posted by the temple trust or endowment board.
